title: A score should show its work. Why ROBUST is the foundation of the Watchdog Score
dek: A 0–100 score is only useful if you can take it apart. ROBUST turns the Watchdog Score into six evidence-backed questions about recourse, overassessment position, burden, uniformity, stability and trajectory, with missing evidence left missing instead of filled with a guess.
meta_description: See how the Watchdog Score uses the ROBUST Framework: six evidence-backed dimensions, explicit weights, source lineage, missing-data rules and sensitivity testing.
author: John Scafide
hero_image_alt: The Watchdog Score and the six ROBUST dimensions: Recourse, Overassessment Position, Burden, Uniformity, Stability and Trajectory.
body_markdown:
A score is easy to build. A score worth putting next to a property is much harder. You can take a handful of numbers, assign some weights, force the answer onto a 0–100 scale and make something that looks authoritative in an afternoon. That is not what we want the Watchdog Score to be. If a number is going to influence what a homeowner investigates, what an agent explains to a client, what an investor notices or what a professional decides deserves a closer look, the number has to earn that responsibility. You should be able to take it apart, see where its inputs came from, understand what is missing and know what would make it move.

Watchdog was never supposed to solve the problem of scattered public records by replacing them with one mystery number. The whole point is the opposite. New Jersey property information is fragmented across assessment records, sales files, equalization data, tax rates, appeal reports, revaluation records and other public sources. One field can be accurate and still tell you almost nothing on its own. The useful question is how those facts relate to each other. A score can make those relationships easier to see, but only if the detail remains underneath it. That is why I think of the Watchdog Score as a decision-orientation signal, not a verdict. It should tell you where to look next, not tell you what to think.

That philosophy is what led to the ROBUST Framework. ROBUST stands for **Recourse, Overassessment Position, Burden, Uniformity, Stability and Trajectory**. These are the six current foundations beneath the property-level Watchdog Score. They were not chosen because the acronym sounded good and then filled with data afterward. They represent six different questions that matter when you are trying to understand a New Jersey property's tax position. Some are about the individual parcel. Some are about the assessment system around it. Some describe today's carrying cost. Others describe whether the conditions around the property appear stable or are moving. Together, they give the headline score enough structure to be useful without trying to stuff every Watchdog data point into one formula.

The public language is deliberate: **The Watchdog Score, powered by the ROBUST Framework.** The Watchdog Score is the result. ROBUST is the methodology underneath it. We do not call it a "ROBUST Score," and we do not describe a home or municipality as "robust." The word is a standard we are setting for the framework itself. It should be multi-dimensional, traceable, reproducible, versioned, tested against alternative assumptions and willing to say when the evidence is not good enough.

## One score, six questions

The current property model is `ROBUST-v1`. With all six dimensions available, the score is conceptually:

`Watchdog Score = 0.10R + 0.20O + 0.30B + 0.15U + 0.15S + 0.10T`

Each component is normalized to a 0–100 scale before aggregation. The current weights are:

- **R · Recourse: 10%**
- **O · Overassessment Position: 20%**
- **B · Burden: 30%**
- **U · Uniformity: 15%**
- **S · Stability: 15%**
- **T · Trajectory: 10%**

Those percentages are not presented as eternal truths. They are the current governed model. We test them, preserve the model version that produced a historical score and require evidence before changing them. That distinction matters. A weighting decision should change because the research supports it, not because a different number looks better on a screen.

The reason these six belong together is that a property-tax position is not one thing. A property can have a manageable current burden but sit in a municipality with poor assessment uniformity. It can appear favorably assessed today but have evidence of a future reset. It can appear pressured against supported value while the available appeal context is weak. ROBUST keeps those different questions separate long enough to understand them, then combines them into one headline signal.

## R · Recourse: what can actually be reviewed?

A pressured condition is incomplete information if there is no context around what a taxpayer can do about it. Recourse is the smallest current weight at 10%, but it belongs in the foundation because the practical ability to review or correct an assessment matters.

New Jersey's Division of Taxation publishes annual county property-tax appeal summaries showing filed appeals and outcomes such as assessments revised, affirmed, stipulated, dismissed or withdrawn. Watchdog uses county-level appeal history as context inside R. The state's own Assessment and Appeals guidance is equally important: every property owner has a right to file an appeal, but the taxpayer has the burden of proving that the assessed value is unreasonable under the true market value or common level range standard.

That is why Recourse is context, not a promise. A county's historical outcome pattern is not "your chance of winning." Different people appeal different properties with different evidence. Some matters settle. Some are dismissed. Some involve procedural issues. The right way to use the data is to understand the environment around review, then look at the evidence for the actual property.

**Exact state sources:** New Jersey Division of Taxation, [Assessment and Appeals](https://www.nj.gov/treasury/taxation/lpt/lpt-appeal.shtml), and the [2025 Summary of Property Tax Appeals](https://www.nj.gov/treasury/taxation/pdf/lpt/appeals2025.pdf).

## O · Overassessment Position: where does this assessment sit against supported value?

This is the individual-property question at the center of a lot of tax-appeal conversations. It is also a place where wording matters.

We call the dimension **Overassessment Position**, not "overassessed" and not simply "fairness." The word *Position* is intentional. Watchdog is measuring where an assessment sits relative to supported value evidence and the Chapter 123 framework. It is not declaring that the property has won an appeal or that an assessment is legally wrong.

New Jersey's common level range is plus or minus 15% of the municipality's average ratio. The Division of Taxation's Chapter 123 definitions give a concrete official example: if the average ratio is 95.41%, the common level range runs from 81.10% to 109.72%. In the state's example, a property with a true value of $100,000 and an assessment of $120,000 has a 120% assessment ratio, which is above the upper limit. The revised taxable value in that example is $95,410, which is the true value multiplied by the average ratio.

Watchdog uses that statutory relationship as a screening framework when it has independent value evidence strong enough to test it. For a simple Watchdog illustration, suppose supported independent value evidence is $500,000 and the applicable municipal ratio is 80%. The ratio-adjusted value is $400,000. The current model's upper Chapter 123 screen is 15% above that, or $460,000. If the parcel is assessed at $485,000, it sits $25,000 above that screening limit. Under the current ROBUST-v1 normalization, O would be about 41 out of 100.

That 41 is not an appeal judgment. It is a signal telling you that the relationship deserves attention and showing you exactly why.

**Exact state sources:** [Chapter 123 Common Level Range Definitions and Calculations](https://www.nj.gov/treasury/taxation/pdf/lpt/chap123/ch123definitions.pdf) and [Assessment and Appeals](https://www.nj.gov/treasury/taxation/lpt/lpt-appeal.shtml).

## B · Burden: what does the property tax actually cost relative to the property?

Burden receives the largest current weight, 30%, for a simple reason: this is the recurring expense the taxpayer actually carries.

Two homes can each have a $12,000 tax bill and be in very different positions. On a supported market value of $400,000, that is a 3.0% annual burden. On a supported value of $800,000, it is 1.5%. The bill is the same. The relationship is not.

ROBUST-v1 currently uses fixed normalization anchors of 1.2% and 3.6%, rather than pretending that the current Watchdog user base is a representative statewide sample. If a property has $12,000 in annual tax and a supported value of $600,000, its effective burden is 2.0%. On the current v1 scale, that maps to roughly 67 out of 100 for B.

The 1.2% and 3.6% anchors are Watchdog model choices, not official New Jersey thresholds. That is exactly the kind of distinction we want to make public. New Jersey publishes general and effective tax rates, assessment lists and equalization data. Watchdog uses governed evidence to create a normalized burden signal on top of those facts.

**Exact state source:** New Jersey Division of Taxation, [Statistical Information](https://www.nj.gov/treasury/taxation/lpt/statdata.shtml), including MOD-IV assessment files, tax rates, equalization data and related local property-tax statistics.

## U · Uniformity: how consistent is the assessment system around the property?

An individual assessment does not exist in a vacuum. It sits inside a municipal assessment roll.

New Jersey publishes Coefficients of Deviation, or CODs, that measure variation in assessment-to-sale ratios. The 2024 Handbook for New Jersey Assessors explains the direction plainly: a higher COD indicates poorer assessment uniformity and a lower COD indicates better uniformity. The handbook identifies 15% as the current acceptable figure, while warning that COD should never be the sole measure of assessment practice.

ROBUST-v1 converts the municipal coefficient into a 0–100 Uniformity component using a current Watchdog normalization range from 7 to 30. A COD of 8 produces a U score of about 96. A COD of 18 produces a U score of about 52.

Again, 7 and 30 are model anchors, not state grades. The state provides the underlying statistical measure and interpretation. Watchdog turns that governed measure into a consistent component scale so it can sit beside the other ROBUST dimensions.

Why does this belong in the score? Because two properties with similar individual assessment positions can face different system-level uncertainty. A parcel in a tightly uniform assessment roll is not in the same context as a parcel in a roll where assessment-to-sale relationships are widely dispersed.

**Exact state sources:** [Handbook for New Jersey Assessors](https://www.nj.gov/treasury/taxation/pdf/assessorshandbook.pdf) and the Division of Taxation's [Coefficient of Deviation tables and definitions](https://www.nj.gov/treasury/taxation/lpt/statdata.shtml).

## S · Stability: is the current assessment environment likely to stay quiet?

A snapshot can look comfortable right before the system changes.

Stability is Watchdog's way of asking whether there is evidence of assessment-reset or revaluation pressure around the municipality. The current model uses a governed revaluation-pressure calculation built from the published ratio level, drift between published and verified-sale ratio evidence, and COD pressure when that measure is available. The pressure calculation is then inverted so lower revaluation pressure produces higher Stability.

Here is a simplified example using the current v1 calculation. Suppose a municipality has a published ratio of 70%, a verified-sale ratio of 62% and a COD of 20. The ratio-level pressure is about 43 on a 0–100 scale, the ratio-drift pressure is 40 and the COD pressure is 25. Under the current 45% / 25% / 30% mix, that produces revaluation pressure around 37, which translates to Stability around 63.

The point is not that Watchdog knows a revaluation will happen. We do not. The point is that New Jersey itself identifies the same family of conditions as relevant when considering revaluation need. The state's revaluation standards specifically discuss assessment-sales ratios, CODs, sales outside the common level range, changes in property characteristics, timing of the last revaluation, record accuracy, appeals and economic changes.

S is therefore a pressure screen, not a prediction of a municipal action date.

**Exact state source:** New Jersey Division of Taxation, [Standards for Valuing Property / Revaluation brochure](https://www.nj.gov/treasury/taxation/pdf/lpt/revaluationbrochure.pdf).

## T · Trajectory: is the property's relationship moving in step with verified market evidence?

Trajectory is the forward-looking parcel dimension. It asks whether the property's assessment relationship is moving in step with verified market evidence relative to the municipality.

This dimension is also the best real-world example of what the ROBUST philosophy means when the easy answer and the defensible answer are not the same.

During our August 2026 calibration work, a broad sale field in the property warehouse initially appeared to make Trajectory available for 166 of the 212 properties in the calibration cohort. That looked like a major improvement. More data. More complete scores. It would have been easy to stop there.

We did not.

We compared those broad sale fields with the governed parcel-level SR-1A subject-sale evidence. Among 10 calibration properties where the governed record resolved cleanly, only one had the same sale year and sale price in the broad property field. Only one matched the sale year, and only two matched the sale price. The broad candidate set also contained 43 pre-2000 sale records whose median exploratory Trajectory score was zero.

That mattered because Trajectory was not a decorative field. In the exploratory run, adding those broad candidates moved scores by 4.918 points on average for the properties carrying T and caused 13.9% band migration. Bad provenance would have materially changed the headline Watchdog Score.

So we rejected the apparent coverage gain. The production scorer was hardened to require governed parcel-level SR-1A subject-sale evidence for Trajectory. If that evidence does not resolve, T stays missing.

That is ROBUST in one sentence: **more data is not automatically better data.** A blank backed by an honest evidence rule is better than a precise-looking number built from the wrong record.

**Exact state data source:** New Jersey Division of Taxation, [Statistical Information and SR-1A Sales Files](https://www.nj.gov/treasury/taxation/lpt/statdata.shtml).

**Watchdog provenance record:** [ROBUST-v1 Trajectory Provenance Decision, August 23, 2026](https://github.com/johnscafide/njtaxrelief/blob/main/property/docs/ROBUST-V1-TRAJECTORY-PROVENANCE-2026-08-23.md).

## Missing evidence should look missing

This is one of the most important rules in the entire score.

If Watchdog does not have one of the ROBUST dimensions, the current model does not quietly fill it with 50 and call that neutral. It does not fill it with zero. It does not assume missing is favorable. It drops the unavailable component, renormalizes the weights that are actually supported and reports evidence coverage separately.

Consider an illustrative property with R = 70, B = 60, U = 80 and S = 50, while O and T are unavailable. The available ROBUST weights total 70%. The current aggregation produces a Watchdog Score of about 64 and evidence coverage of 70%, which is currently classified as medium confidence.

Now pretend we filled the missing O and T values with 50. The same property would score about 60. We would have changed the headline number by inventing two facts we did not know.

Our first calibration pass tested this issue across the persisted cohort. Keeping the current renormalization rule reproduced stored scores exactly. Filling missing dimensions with 50 moved scores by 2.86 points on average. Filling missing values with zero moved scores by 17.02 points on average and changed score bands for 94.8% of the sample. Filling them with 100 moved scores by 11.35 points and changed bands for 93.9%.

The takeaway is not that renormalization is perfect forever. The takeaway is that missingness is part of the evidence. We should not hide it.

Long term, some scores should probably say **Insufficient evidence** rather than display an unqualified number. We are deliberately not forcing a numeric-only cutoff yet because our calibration work shows that composition matters. A score with 70% coverage can be very different depending on which 30% is missing.

## We tested the weights. The result was to leave them alone.

There is another part of the philosophy that matters to me: not changing something can be a research result.

The August 22 ROBUST-v1 calibration reproduced all 336 persisted canonical observations exactly from their stored component evidence. The latest-property cohort contained 212 properties with a mean score of 60.2 and mean evidence coverage of 71.6%. We perturbed each dimension's weight by plus or minus 20%, ran leave-one-component-out tests and examined band and rank movement.

Small weight perturbations were generally stable. Burden was the strongest ranking lever in the observed cohort. Removing it entirely moved scores by 7.684 points on average. Overassessment Position had less effect across the full cohort because it was available on only 21 properties at the time, but where O existed its removal moved individual scores by as much as about 20.6 points.

Most importantly, the sample was not representative enough to justify a new model. The persisted cohort had no Trajectory evidence at all and limited O coverage. So we kept R10 / O20 / B30 / U15 / S15 / T10. We did not create ROBUST-v2 just to make it look as if calibration had produced a change.

Since then, governed SR-1A subject matching has improved, and our non-writing calibration work has expanded real O and T evidence. But the governed subset is still concentrated geographically and by property class. The current conclusion remains the same: keep the v1 weights while the evidence base broadens.

That is the standard I want Watchdog to keep. A model version should change because the evidence earns the change.

**Watchdog calibration source:** [ROBUST-v1 Calibration Decision, August 22, 2026](https://github.com/johnscafide/njtaxrelief/blob/main/property/docs/ROBUST-V1-CALIBRATION-2026-08-22.md).

## Why six foundations instead of twenty, fifty or five hundred?

Watchdog can support hundreds and eventually thousands of property data points. That does not mean the flagship score should absorb all of them.

The better structure is hierarchical. Official source facts sit at the bottom. Watchdog normalizes them without changing their meaning. Governed derived markers sit above those facts. Selected markers support the six ROBUST dimensions. The six dimensions support the Watchdog Score. Confidence and eventually Momentum sit beside the score, not hidden inside it.

That structure is easier to explain, test and improve. A permit marker can matter to a specific professional workflow without becoming part of the tax-position score. An investor can care about carry-cost volatility without pretending it belongs in Recourse. An attorney can care deeply about appeal evidence strength without turning every legal nuance into a top-level component.

The flagship score should be disciplined enough that a user can remember what it means.

**R** asks about practical review context.  
**O** asks where this specific assessment sits.  
**B** asks what the taxpayer is carrying.  
**U** asks how consistent the surrounding assessment system is.  
**S** asks whether that system appears stable.  
**T** asks where the individual property's relationship is heading against verified market evidence.

That is a coherent foundation. More fields can improve the evidence under those questions without turning the top line into an indecipherable formula.

## What the Watchdog Score is not

A Watchdog Score of 82 does not mean a house is better than one with a 62. A 38 does not mean a neighborhood is bad. A town with pressured assessment conditions is not being graded as a community or as a government.

The score is not a desirability score. It is not a school score. It is not a safety score. It is not a political score. Protected personal characteristics do not belong in the core ROBUST model, and the score should never be tuned to make a municipality, customer, advertiser or political actor happier with the result.

The score also should not make a high-stakes decision by itself. It can help a homeowner decide what to investigate, help a professional prioritize review, or help Watchdog surface unusual relationships. It does not determine an appeal, appraisal, loan, insurance decision, legal right or where someone should live.

That boundary is not a disclaimer added after the model. It is part of the model's design.

## The larger idea: a common language that can travel with a property

The long-term opportunity is larger than a badge on a dashboard.

If the Watchdog Score is going to appear in reports, professional workflows, APIs, integrations, Watchdog Atlas or eventually beside other familiar property facts, the number has to carry its explanation with it. A future line like `Watchdog Score 72 · Confidence 91 · Momentum +4` only means something if a user can click through to the six ROBUST dimensions, then continue down to the actual evidence and source vintage.

That is the philosophy in practical terms: the number should never be the end of the analysis. It should be the front door.

The OECD and European Commission's *Handbook on Constructing Composite Indicators* makes the same broader point about composite measures. Indicator selection, missing-data treatment, normalization, weighting and aggregation all involve choices that can materially affect the result. The handbook recommends uncertainty and sensitivity analysis to understand how robust a composite result is to those choices.

We take that seriously. If the framework is called ROBUST, robustness cannot just be branding. It has to be something we keep testing.

The Watchdog Score should become easier to recognize as it grows, but never harder to question. You should know where the number came from. You should know what is missing. You should know what version produced it. You should be able to see the strongest drivers. And when the evidence is not good enough, Watchdog should be willing to say so.

That is what I want the score to earn: not blind trust, but understandable trust.

faq.q: What does ROBUST stand for in the Watchdog Score?
faq.a: ROBUST stands for Recourse, Overassessment Position, Burden, Uniformity, Stability and Trajectory. These are the six evidence-backed dimensions under the current property-level Watchdog Score.

faq.q: Is the Watchdog Score the same thing as a ROBUST Score?
faq.a: No. The Watchdog Score is the public 0–100 result. The ROBUST Framework is the methodology that explains the score. The preferred language is “The Watchdog Score, powered by the ROBUST Framework.”

faq.q: What happens if Watchdog does not have all six ROBUST dimensions?
faq.a: ROBUST-v1 omits missing dimensions and renormalizes the weights that are actually supported. It separately reports evidence coverage and confidence rather than quietly filling missing evidence with a made-up neutral, positive or negative value.

faq.q: Does a low Watchdog Score mean a house or town is bad?
faq.a: No. The score is a property-tax-position signal, not a desirability grade on a home, neighborhood, family, municipality or government. A lower score means the measured tax and assessment conditions are more pressured under the named model and evidence set.

faq.q: Can the Watchdog Score tell me whether I should file a property-tax appeal?
faq.a: Not by itself. ROBUST can surface assessment position, appeal context and supporting evidence that deserve review, but New Jersey places the burden of proof on the taxpayer and an actual appeal depends on the property's evidence and applicable law.
